title: Decision Trees & Random Forests
subtitle: How a tree asks questions, why it memorizes, and how averaging hundreds of decorrelated trees turns a fragile model into the most reliable workhorse in tabular ML

objectives.title: Grow and Read a Decision Tree
objectives.description: Gini impurity in plain English, greedy binary splits, and plot_tree — a model you can print on one page and hand to a manager.

objectives.title: See Overfitting in a Tree
objectives.description: An unlimited tree reaches 99% training accuracy by carving a leaf for every quirky booking. max_depth and min_samples_leaf are its regularization knobs.

objectives.title: Build a Random Forest and Explain Why It Works
objectives.description: Bootstrap rows, sample features at every split, average the votes. Decorrelated trees cancel each other's errors — variance reduction you can watch happen.

objectives.title: Measure Importance Honestly
objectives.description: Impurity importance is biased toward high-cardinality columns; permutation importance on held-out data is not. Partial dependence shows the shape of the effect.

agenda.title: HW3 Debrief & Meet the Data: Hotel Bookings
agenda.description: Threshold choices from your HW3 submissions — the range was 0.18 to 0.42, and the best memo explained why. Then the competition dataset: 83,573 hotel reservations from a city and a resort hotel in Portugal, 37% canceled, 32 columns — two of which are leaks.
bulletPoints: reservation_status and reservation_status_date are the outcome in disguise: drop them or your leaderboard score is fiction
assigned_room_type vs. reserved_room_type: a mismatch is known only at check-in — think about whether that's leakage too

agenda.title: How a Tree Asks Questions
agenda.description: 'Is lead_time > 90 days?' 'Is deposit_type non-refundable?' A tree is a flowchart learned from data: at each node it picks the question that most reduces impurity. Gini = probability that two random guests from this node disagree on cancellation.
bulletPoints: Greedy: the best split now, not the best tree overall
plot_tree on a depth-3 model: the whole cancellation story on one screen

agenda.title: Watching a Tree Overfit
agenda.description: Depth 1 → 3 → 6 → unlimited. Training accuracy climbs to 99%; test accuracy peaks around depth 8–10 and then falls. The tree has memorized the training bookings. A validation curve over max_depth makes the sweet spot visible.
bulletPoints: Trees need no scaling and handle mixed types — but a single tree is high-variance: change 5% of the data and the tree changes shape
min_samples_leaf=50 is often a better knob than max_depth for business data

agenda.title: From One Tree to a Forest
agenda.description: Bagging: fit 500 trees, each on a bootstrap sample, average their votes — variance drops. Random forest adds the twist: at every split, only a random subset of features is eligible, so the trees disagree more and the average improves more. Out-of-bag score: a free validation set built from the rows each tree never saw.
bulletPoints: Forests are hard to overfit by adding trees; n_estimators=500 is rarely worse than 100, just slower
Hotel bookings: a depth-limited single tree reaches ~0.90 AUC; the forest reaches ~0.95 with no tuning

agenda.title: Which Features Matter — and How
agenda.description: feature_importances_ (impurity) vs. permutation_importance on the test set — and the high-cardinality trap: a hashed ID column ranks #1 by impurity and dead last by permutation. Then PartialDependenceDisplay: how cancellation probability actually moves with lead time.
bulletPoints: Permutation importance answers 'if I scrambled this column, how much would the model get worse?' — the honest question
Partial dependence for lead_time on hotel data rises steeply to ~100 days and flattens: a curve a revenue manager can price

agenda.title: Wrap-Up & Competition Check-In
agenda.description: Every team should have a leak-free pipeline and a forest submission by tonight. Next week, gradient boosting — the model that will probably win — and the tabular foundation models that might beat it.
bulletPoints: Leaderboard closes Sun Nov 8, 11:59 PM; final-project proposals due Mon Nov 9 on Canvas

steps.title: Two importances

codeBlock.code:
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

url = 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/harslan/isom-835/master/public/data/hotel_bookings.csv'
df = pd.read_csv(url).sample(30_000, random_state=835)          # subsample for speed in class
leaks = ['reservation_status', 'reservation_status_date', 'assigned_room_type']
X = df.drop(columns=['is_canceled'] + leaks)
X = X.apply(lambda c: c.astype('category').cat.codes if c.dtype == object else c).fillna(-1)
X['noise'] = np.random.default_rng(835).normal(size=len(X))       # a column with zero signal
y = df['is_canceled']
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=835)

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, min_samples_leaf=5, oob_score=True, n_jobs=-1, random_state=835)
rf.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f'OOB AUC-ish (accuracy): {rf.oob_score_:.3f}   test AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_te, rf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]):.3f}')

imp = pd.DataFrame({'impurity': rf.feature_importances_}, index=X.columns)
imp['permutation'] = permutation_importance(rf, X_te, y_te, scoring='roc_auc', n_repeats=5, random_state=835, n_jobs=-1).importances_mean
print(imp.sort_values('permutation', ascending=False).head(8).round(4))
print('noise column rank by impurity:', int((imp['impurity'] > imp.loc['noise', 'impurity']).sum()) + 1)

activities.discussionNote: The forest reaches an AUC around 0.94 on a 30k-row slice with no tuning and no scaling — that is why it is the first serious model most practitioners reach for. But look at the importance table: deposit_type, lead_time, and country lead by permutation, while the pure-noise column sits surprisingly high by impurity. Impurity importance rewards columns that offer many split points, not columns that predict. If you report feature importance to a manager, report the permutation version.

takeaways.text: A decision tree is a flowchart learned greedily from data: interpretable, scale-free, and high-variance. Depth and min_samples_leaf are its brakes; a single tree rarely ships.
A random forest is variance reduction by averaging decorrelated trees — bootstrap rows, sample features at every split. Hard to overfit by adding trees; the out-of-bag score is a free validation set.
Impurity importance lies about high-cardinality columns; permutation importance on held-out data does not. Partial dependence shows the shape of an effect, which is what a manager actually asks for.
